disposition.note:
Your diagnosis: Acute viral gastroenteritis ("stomach flu")

This is a common infection of the stomach and intestines, usually caused by a virus. It causes watery diarrhea, nausea, and sometimes stomach cramps. It usually gets better on its own within a few days to about a week. Antibiotics do not help and are not needed for a viral infection.

Stay hydrated — this is the most important thing
Drink small amounts of fluid often, even if you feel nauseated. Sip rather than gulp.
Best choices: oral rehydration solutions (such as Pedialyte), water, broth, and diluted juice. Sports drinks are okay if diluted with water.
Try to drink a cup of fluid after each loose stool.
Avoid alcohol and large amounts of caffeine, which can worsen dehydration.

Eating
You do not need to stop eating. Once nausea improves, start with small, bland, easy-to-digest foods (such as bananas, rice, toast, crackers, applesauce, potatoes, plain chicken).
Avoid dairy, greasy or fried foods, and very sugary foods for a few days, as these can make diarrhea worse. Milk sugar (lactose) can be harder to digest for a short time after this type of illness.
Return to your normal diet gradually as you feel better.

Medications
For diarrhea — Loperamide (Imodium) 2 mg: Take 2 capsules (4 mg) by mouth after your first loose stool, then 1 capsule (2 mg) after each additional loose stool. Do not take more than 8 mg (4 capsules) in one day. Do NOT use it if you develop a fever or see blood in your stool, and stop it if you are not improving after 2 days.
For nausea — Ondansetron (Zofran) 4 mg: Take 1 tablet by mouth every 8 hours as needed for nausea or vomiting. Let the office know if nausea keeps you from drinking fluids.
You may use acetaminophen (Tylenol) for aches or discomfort. Take as directed on the label.

Prevent spreading it to others
Wash your hands well with soap and water, especially after using the bathroom and before eating or preparing food. Hand sanitizer alone may not kill this type of virus.
Do not prepare food for others while you are sick and for at least 2 days after symptoms stop. This is especially important because you work at a daycare — stay home until you have had no diarrhea or vomiting for at least 24–48 hours.
Clean and disinfect contaminated surfaces.

Come back or seek care right away if you have:
Signs of dehydration: very dark urine or not urinating, dizziness, lightheadedness, dry mouth, or a fast heartbeat
Blood in your stool or black, tarry stools
A fever of 102°F (38.9°C) or higher
Severe or worsening stomach pain, especially if it moves to the lower right side
Vomiting that prevents you from keeping any fluids down
Diarrhea that lasts longer than 7 days or keeps coming back
Confusion or extreme weakness

Follow-up
Contact the office if your symptoms are not improving after a few days, if they return, or if you have any of the warning signs above.
